newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian budget seen helping textiles industry.
newsitem.headline: Indian budget seen helping textiles industry.

text.p: India's recession-hit textile industry is expected to get a boost from the country's federal budget, analysts said on Sunday.
"The budget came at the right time to help the textile industry," said Indian Cotton Mills' Federation (ICMF) secretary-general M.P. Gajaria.
The federal budget for 1997/98 (April/March) was presented to parliament by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Friday.
The textile industry, India's oldest, accounts for a fifth of the country's total industrial production and about 30 percent of its foreign exchange earnings.
The industry provides direct and indirect jobs to about 20 million people and contributes nearly 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion) in domestic revenue.
The budget proposed to reduce excise duty on polyester fibre yarn by 11.5 percent to 34.5 percent and polyester staple fibre by 2.3 percent to 20.7 percent.
The budget reduced customs duty on capital goods by five percent to 20 percent. It also proposed a technology upgrade fund for the textile industry.
"These measures will significantly increase the demand for textiles," said Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive of Lloyds Securities.
ICMF's Gajaria said the budget had provided a level playing field between small-scale spinning units and cotton yarn mills by imposing a uniform excise duty on both sectors.
"It's a step in the right direction," he said.
He said the reduction in customs duty on capital goods would help textile units upgrade equipment and improve competitiveness.
Some business leaders, however, felt the budget had not gone far enough to help the textile industry.
"There is need to reduce excise duty on fabrics to boost demand. But it had not been done," said Bombay Mill Owners' Association secretary-general V.Y. Tamhane.
There are 54 textile mills in Bombay, 22 of them owned by the government and the remainder by the private sector.
Tamhane said the Bombay mills, which made a profit of 1.22 billion rupees ($34 million) in 1991/92, slipped into the red by 1995/96 when they suffered a total loss of 1.3 billion.
Another budgetary proposal that found favour with the textile industry has been the government's decision to allow futures trading in cotton.
"It's a very good step. We will be able to cover cotton for a longer period," Gajaria said. "It's a sort of an insurance for the textile industry." ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
